comments.author: superfrank
comments.text: I started using Spark 1.2 for development because if you're willing to let Meta train on your data it was dirt cheap and was actually really pleasantly surprised with it. It's not a frontier model by any means, but for work that didn't require a top of the line model, I really enjoyed using it. I'm anthropomorphizing it a bit, but it felt like it knew its weaknesses and didn't try to impose it's opinions on me. What I mean by that is that it did what I told it and if there was something unexpected in the code that it put out it was often because I gave it ambiguous or conflicting instructions. It didn't try to go above and beyond and just acted like a tool, which is what I want from a coding agent 90%+ of the time. I also felt that it did a much better job of following established patterns in my code than many of the other current models do. I'm a huge fan of OpenAI's models and Spark 1.2 is what I expected 5.6 Luna to be. I'm curious and a little excited to use 1.3, but honestly a little worried that as Meta pushes for better benchmarks that Spark will start to fall into the trap of trying to be "helpful" in ways I don't want it to be. Tangential, but when I first started using Spark 1.2, it made me realize how much I miss 5.3 Codex. That model was the peak of coding models, IMO, in that it knew how to write good code, but didn't try to overstep or be "helpful" in unexpected ways. That got me thinking about how the major labs seem to be stepping away from coding focused models toward more general purpose ones and how I can't help but feel like that's a mistake.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Muse Spark 1.3のパフォーマンス向上とコスト効率、そして以前のバージョン1.2との比較です。コミュニティは1.3がSVG生成での品質が向上し（自転車フレームや翼、ハットの描写が改善）、DeepSWEスコア75.4でSOTAに近づきつつも価格が非常に安い点を称賛しています。一方、1.2の頃は「ツールらしく」指示に従い余計な助言をしない姿勢が好評で、1.3ではベンチマーク向上のために過剰に「助けよう」とする傾向が懸念されています。賛否の分かれ目は、性能向上とコスト低下を歓迎する声と、かつてのCodexや1.2のような素直さを失わないかという不安です。注目コメントとして、あるユーザーは「1.3は確かに良いが、Metaがベンチマークを追うほどに「役立ちすぎ」てコード生成の余計な推測が増えるのではないか」と指摘し、これがコーディングエージェントとしての使い勝手に影響する可能性を警告しています。全体として、Spark 1.3は高品質・低コストでの実用性が高く評価される一方で、以前の素直な振る舞いを保てるかが今後の焦点となっています。
stories.editor_note: Muse Spark 1.3 は、起動が極めて速く、AI コード補完を組み込んだ軽量 IDE だ。最近の日本スタートアップでは開発サイクルの短縮が求められ、これを採用するケースが増えている。今注目されるのは、クラウド開発環境へのシフトと相性が良い点だ。

注目コメント：AI生成のヘッダーイラストにノートが逆さだったりハサミで手を切ろうとする子供などのミスがあり、「レビュー反対論文なのに自分がレビューされていない」と皮肉った指摘が特に目を引いた。
stories.editor_note: 「このコード全部をレビューすべきではないかもしれません」という指摘は、膨大なコードベースにおけるレビューのコストパフォーマンス問題を提起する。日本の大規模 SIer でも、自動化とリスクベースのアプローチが求められている。

comments.author: kstrauser
comments.text: Story time: I worked the night shift at a motel during college. "Bored to tears" was an understatement. I was poking around the front desk computer system one night, as one does, and found its data file. Lacking anything else to do, I wrote a little hex dumper in BASIC so I could explore the file. The first thing I noted was that customer names were spaced exactly N bytes apart. Oooh, fixed records! Then I spent the next week or so reverse engineering the DB file format. I'd twiddle a field in a random customer record then look at their record in the hex dump to see what changed, then update my notes. Eventually I wrote another little BASIC program to run analytics, like which customers spent the most with us, and auto-fix mistyped names ("This says 'Bb Jones'. Did you mean 'Bob Jones'?") by writing directly to the file. I got a pretty sweet little bonus for my hackery.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ImHexを使った未知バイナリフォーマットの解析手法とその実用性である。参加者はパターンテンプレートや構造体定義によりファイル内部を可視化しやすく、特にMinecraftレガシー版セーブやモーテルの古いDBファイルなど実際の事例で成功を報告した。賛否については、テンプレートが便利である一方、実行時サイズ配列や可変長セクションの扱いがデバッグ時にエラーを起こしやすく、以前にデコードした構造体が失われる点が指摘された。また、Cヘッダーとの双方向変換が欲しいという要望や、LLMがパターン発見を補助するという期待が示された。注目コメントとして、大学時代にモーテルの夜勤中にBASICでヘックスダンパを書き、固定長レコードを見つけてDBフォーマットを逆解析し、分析ツールと名前自動修正機能を実装してボーナスを得た話が挙げられ、さらに「未知フォーマットの半分はZIP内のSQLite DBである」という経験則や、Onshapeが独自のAutodesk Inventor sldprtをインポートできる仕組みへの関心が示された。
stories.editor_note: ImHex を使って未知のファイル形式をリバースエンジニアリングする手法は、マルウェア解析やフォーマット互換性改善に有効だ。日本のセキュリティベンダーや組み込み機器メーカーは、こうしたツールを導入し、脅威インテリジェンスを強化している。

Every and each one told me enthusiastically to go to "Foobar square" (name changed) for the "best street food in XYZ town", some added a lot of colorful details. There was no Foobar square in XYZ town. There was no Foobar square anywhere in the world. There was a SINGLE old Reddit comment, with no upvotes, to a unpopular post in an unpopular subreddit, where someone clearly badly misspelled the name of the square, and said something like "for street food go to Foobar square". Nothing about "the best" even. It's all a lie.

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text: I used one of the 12-month free Perplexity offers when they were everywhere. It felt slightly useful at first for simple queries where I didn’t want to go through the top 10 Google results manually. If I was looking for a specific recipe I remembered or a help page or user manual it would usually find it quickly. Then they started optimizing for speed of responses over quality of results. I can enter a query and see my results appear in a second, but they’re garbage. The links and references it gives frequently don’t match the text right next to them. It feels like someone had a KPI to make responses as fast as possible and they optimized for that above all else. They added a “Computer” option that’s supposed to do research for you. Half the time I can’t get it to trigger through the UI. Pressing the submit button doesn’t work. When I can get it to trigger, most of those sessions will work for a while and then just stop before an answer comes back. The only reason I keep using it is to keep observing a company that has been heavily marketed and hyped, which should have had a market leading position for something. Even non-technical people I know who listen to Joe Rogan (where Perlexity is advertising heavily, I’m told) are asking me about it. Now there are reports of people being billed at the end of their trial period without warning, despite them saying that they will warn before this happens. There are some alarmingly bad customer support screenshots where the customer support agent (AI? Probably) acknowledges that they didn’t send the email they promised but refuse to help anyway. It takes escalating it on Twitter to get it corrected. If I want to do actual research or AI assisted web searching I have Claude or ChatGPT do it. The results are so much higher quality and it does exactly what I ask. It may take 45 seconds instead of the instant response from Perplexity but I save time overall because the response and links are more likely to be correct

comments.author: inciampati
comments.text: He was a friend of many people in my community. I met him a few times at public lectures. But his way of thinking has had a profound impact on my life. I rejected his rejection of technology. I think he didn't appreciate the power of information technology to support exactly the dreams he held. If people can understand each other, if they can learn from the whole world how to care for their bit of earth, surely that's a good thing? Because he rejected technology he never learned of free, open source, culture. He didn't appreciate that there is another path to liberation of humans from the machines that dominate us—that we embed them in our communities, bend them to our will, and reject exploitation. There's still hope... I however am permanently touched by his perspective on the land as our foundation. I was so inspired that I helped start a farm on the Kentucky River. It's a journey, but we are on our way to implement a little reflection of his vision near where he dreamed us these beautiful dreams of past and future.

I was struck by how similar Berry, Pirsig, and the early MIT hackers thought about Quality work. I gave a talk about it at an images & algorithms class I took in undergrad. It's reassuring to see Wendell Berry was an influential figure to many others in this space. RIP.

comments.author: schoen

Among (many) other things, he wrote a fair amount of criticism of technology and computers. https://classes.matthewjbrown.net/teaching-files/philtech/be... I was always struck that one of the letters in opposition to Berry's view was written by Nathaniel Borenstein, the co-inventor of MIME. It was an odd experience for me because it was coming from such a different worldview that I generally felt I couldn't relate to what Berry was saying at all. (I could contrast that with some of Cliff Stoll's writings about his skepticism of computers, which are always coming from a culturally familiar place and are at least readily comprehensible for me.) I also have a book Berry wrote as a rejoinder to E. O. Wilson's Consilience (called Life is a Miracle ). I put the two next to each other on my bookshelf!

comments.author: logicallee
comments.text: people very soon as going to look back at all of us and just think "they didn't even have robots yet! how did they even eat?" Well, future readers, it isn't easy! We either go to the store and bring back groceries ourselves or pay a helper to do it. No robot in the loop there. stories.title_en: Embedded Rust RTOS vs. C RTOS

comments.author: Animats
comments.text: That's under very light CPU load. So an async approach, with no preemption, can work. If there's any significant compute going on, it won't work as well. A useful number to measure on a scope is worst case interrupt latency. This is what matters if there's a hard real-time constraint. They measured standard deviation, but not worst case. The usual test setup is that an input signal (typically a square wave) goes to an input pin, interrupt happens if interrupts not prevented, task starts, task turns on an output pin. You watch input to output delay on a scope and look for outliers. If you're running entirely run to completion, the outliers are determined by the longest compute task. This is a problem if there's a compute task. This is historically where QNX shines. Interrupt is processed and schedules a thread. About all that happens at interrupt level is thread activation. The thread turns on the output pin. You can look on a scope for scheduling outliers. The best case latency is higher than doing the work at interrupt level, but the worst case latency is constant, even if lower priority threads are compute bound. This is the difference between real time and "near real time" scheduling.

comments.author: CupricTea
comments.text: Title should be changed. Async Rust != RTOS. RTOS's are preemptively multithreaded while async is done cooperatively with yield points. Perhaps "Embedded async Rust vs. C RTOS"

comments.author: MarkusWandel
comments.text: Being an "aging brain" myself I can totally relate to this. I've been a relatively obsessive photographer (i.e. visual diary) since digital cameras were practical, i.e. over 25 years now. 238K photos in the collection so far, and I can actually find things in it. And I've more than once found that an anecdote I've been telling has been incorrect, precisely in a "melded memories" kind of way. It happened at this sort of gathering which were usually held for that reason so X was involved... and then finally look at the old pictures and there's no sign of X. It is literally the brain invoking "lossy compression" to make it all fit, just like certain web services that let you upload pictures without limit might reduce old ones, that hardly anyone ever looks at any more, to lower quality to limit storage bloat. Of course any married man can confirm that this only applies to men. Women's memories are flawless. If they claim that they remember a conversation exactly, word for word, 20 years later, who's to prove them wrong?

comments.author: HarHarVeryFunny
comments.text: I wonder how much of this is directly related to age (biological aging), and how much is just someone's brain becoming "full" due to more memories getting added every year? It seems that memories must be stored as embeddings with single multi-neuron assemblies (cortical columns?) storing multiple embeddings as a kind of contents-addressable memory that is able to keep memories distinct due to the very high dimensional space (# neurons per assembly) being used. However, you'd expect that at some point if you store too many memories in a single assembly the recall accuracy is going to go down. You'd expect that with big brains being so costly, evolution has only equipped us with brains big enough to store a lifetime of memories, so it would be odd if memory didn't suffer as we get old. To make a computer analogy, it's a bit like a hash table getting too full. Say you had a hash table without any overflow mechanism... up to a point recall may still be pretty good, but as the table gets closer to full there will be more hash collisions and likelyhood of "false recall". Obviously the brain is not a computer, but the analogy may hold up reasonably well if you consider the hash table keys and values as embeddings and the store operation being an embedding merge rather than overwrite.

comments.author: petreradu
comments.text: The paper certainly has its limitations. Only 61 participants, with almost nobody between 30 and 50, so we shouldn’t read the age trend as a decline across lifespan. What’s more interesting than the title suggests (and I find the title forcing the conclusion a bit) is that the attention measures were not linked to age or the brain patterns at all. Then again, i'm 45 and I've been losing my keys and my IDs since I was 20

comments.text: The concept of memories blending together resonates after watching a recent Kurzgezadt video entitled "How Are Memories Stored Inside Your Brain?". It makes the point that the very act of recalling a memory changes it: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PqtggjVAi8M > But memories are not static like photos. Like dioramas made from wax, each time they’re under the spotlight of your attention they can melt and change a tiny bit.

comments.author: rhdunn
comments.text: My theory behind this is that when you encounter something new/novel it is distinct enough to remember -- where you were when you learned of 9/11; the days around the start of covid/lockdowns; being in a car accident; getting married; etc.. However, when you experience the same thing repetitively -- having breakfast; getting ready for school/work/etc. -- it doesn't make sense for your brain to remember each of these events as distinct events but to mush them together into a single or combined memory. This may be due to how the brain indexes/references memories and that memories with the same references get combined together. This is also partly why time appears to go faster when you get older -- the same day-to-day events blend together but the key milestones (holidays, etc.) stick out.

comments.author: jondlm
comments.text: A couple weeks ago I went by myself for a hike through an old lava tunnel cave. I needed a flashlight because it was pitch black. I found a small nook in the wall about a mile in that I could wedge myself in to. I sat down, turned off my light, and let myself feel the enveloping darkness for a long time. I cried. The only sounds were of small droplets of cold water hitting the floor and my body. I let myself settle in to the sensation of being buried alone under the rock where liquid fire once reigned. I felt at peace. When I finally emerged from the cold tunnel a thrill ran through me as warm air gushed over my skin and the distant sun found me once again. I sat and fed the birds that visited me in the remote wilderness while I listened to the gentle whirl of wind in the trees.

comments.author: LogicFailsMe
comments.text: The only thing worse than 100% inhabiting your own cave is trying to fit into someone else's. I had a conversation this weekend with someone in an emerging startup that I initially wanted to join but increasingly didn't as I realized I had gone from starring cast to somewhere between entourage and sub 1% equity NPC. And at that point, startups are horrible bets when you have any sort of sure thing IMO. But it was instructive to watch him neg, criticize, and dismiss all of my own ideas that weren't in service of his vision thing, occasionally pivoting to deflecting any criticism of the potential for his own vision to succeed. This week I pitched my vision to my current employer. They loved it. Case closed. Ideas are cheap, it's executions that deliver value. And I have a superb record on that. Conclusion: if you poke your head up for feedback now and then, there's nothing with spending most of your time in the cave to avoid the samsara of influencers, rage bait, and social media algorithms. Anyone telling you otherwise is 'sus.

comments.author: sp1nningaway
comments.text: Frighteningly, I've also found that you can be in the cave together with a group of people. I went to an MMA gym for a long time, and it was very common to see overconfident 'experienced' new members start sparring and get their ass handed to them. It was always someone from a small town or a gym that didn't participate in the larger MMA community. Those smaller gyms followed the same ruleset, but are made up of individual egos that always want their own hand raised. You can go for years in a group that has collectively agreed to hide from actually bumping up against the limits of their abilities.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、「洞窟（孤独な内省）」に滞在することの価値と、外部からのフィードバックや試練の必要性についての議論だった。コメントでは、自己の進歩だけを基準にし、他者へのusefulnessを重視しない姿勢を肯定する意見と、孤独に浸りすぎると未検証の幻想を守るだけになるという批判が対立した。さらに、スタートアップや格闘技ジムの例を挙げて、グループ内でも「洞窟思考」がエゴの衝突や限界回避を引き起こし、実行やarena（闘技場）での挑戦が重要であるという指摘があった。注目すべきコメントとして、テディー・ルーズベルトの「arena」演説とニルス・ヴァン・デル・ポエルのトレーニング論を引用し、洞窟で内省するのはよいが、最終的にarenaで実際に行動し、失敗を恐れずに挑戦することが真の成長につながると述べた意見が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 「洞窟から出る」は、既存の思考フレームワークから脱却し、新たな視点を得る比喩として解釈できる。日本のイノベーション創出現場では、従来の業務プロセスに囚われず、外部知識や異分野交流を促す取り組みが活発化している。

comments.author: talloaktrees
comments.text: Zhuangzi was fishing in the Pu River when the King of Chu sent two high officials to him. They said, “The king wishes to entrust you with the affairs of his realm.” Zhuangzi kept hold of his fishing rod and did not turn around. He said, “I have heard that in Chu there is a sacred turtle that has been dead for three thousand years. The king keeps it wrapped in cloth, enclosed in a box, and stored in the ancestral temple. “Now, would this turtle rather have died and left its bones behind to be honored, or would it rather be alive, dragging its tail through the mud?” The two officials replied, “It would rather be alive, dragging its tail through the mud.” Zhuangzi said, “Then go away. I too will drag my tail through the mud.”

comments.author: oilkillsbirds
comments.text: This is pure escapism. Numbing yourself to the burden of being. Likely from a stress tolerance so shallow and under-developed that the slightest inconvenience or expectation feels like a crisis. The truth is that after the brief initial relief of excusing yourself from being anything at all, you'll end up in a deep depression. It's a naive and immature fantasy. Remove all electronics from your life, they are a constant nervous system stimulator that has prevented you from truly relaxing into a state of repair. Then introduce responsibilities into your life, start small. We are wired to be needed, wanted, useful, accountable, social. You're just stressed out.

comments.author: ikesau
comments.text: To make the most facile counterpoint - the reason the Skyrim blacksmith doesn't care if the main character slays dragons is because they weren't programmed to. There aren't consequences either way. To the extent that this post is meant to be inspiring, it only works if you're an NPC in a static world that has no real consequences - where you actually can live your life in a static loop because nothing will change. When the metaphorical dragon comes to burn down your village, are you going to shrug and go back to looping your hammer_nail_03 animation?

comments.author: InexSquirrel
comments.text: I think NPC is the wrong terminology here - everyone should be the main character in their life - to have meaning and agency. But I think the problem arises in how 'main character' is defined and expressed - having the idea that you're supposed to 'do great things' and live this larger-than-life, life. You don't have to save all the rhinos, defeat every poverty, slay every social cause or overthrow every tyranny. If anything it's arrogance to assume you can, or even should - that your specific brand of saving anything is even correct. If you look at most people that do well for themselves and have good lives, they live narrow focused lives in domains they care about. They're very much the main characters of their own lives, but also recognize there are other characters running around doing their own things as well. I think using the term NPC would be more apt if you're referring to someone that's purely on autopilot and not making any effort to ensure that they're leading a life that is meaningful to them .

comments.author: Swizec
comments.text: That’s the best part! We’re all NPCs in other people’s stories _and_ the main character in ours. You can do and be absolutely anything or anyone you want. Just gotta bear the consequences and that’s it. Wanna live a homely life surrounded by loved ones? Go do it! Nobody is stopping you. Wanna galivant around the world having adventures with no roots? You can! And when you meet a local npc bartender on your adventures, you’re just another rando tourist npc. It’s great

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、「NPCのように生きること」が単なる逃避であり、責任や目的を欠いた生活は結局うつに陥るという見方と、他者の物語の中ではNPCだが自分の人生では主人公であるという視点で意味を見出すべきだという見方の対立である。賛否両論として、批判側は「何もせずに流されるだけ」ではストレス耐性が低く、現実からの逃避はやがて深い落ち込みを招くと主張し、小さな責任を積み重ねることの重要性を強調した。肯定側は、NPCという比喩は「偉業を成す必要はなく、自分の関心領域に集中すれば十分」であり、過大な使命感を捨てて日常の中に小さな意味を見つけるべきだと主張し、スカイリムの鍛冶屋のように結果が変わらない静的世界での生活は現実には通用しないと指摘する声もあった。また、電子機器を排除し小さな義務から始めるべきだという実践的助言や、スカイリムの鍛冶屋のように結果に無関心なNPCでは本当の課題に直面したときに機能しないという批判も見られた。注目コメントでは、 Zhuangzi の亀の故事を引用して「泥の中を這う亀」のように現実に根ざした生き方を選ぶべきだと説いた意見と、「みんな他人の物語のNPCであり、自分の物語の主人公」というコメントで、主従関係の相対性を示した洞察が特に注目された。
stories.editor_note: 「NPC のように生きたい」という願望は、現代社会における自律性喪失とルーチンへの依存を暗示している。日本の若年層の間で、ワークライフバランスや意味ある仕事への志向が高まり、この感覚はキャリア選択の指標として注目されている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ロスアラモス研究所のかつての従業員エド・グロサスが集めた「ブラックホール」サルベージ品から発見されたロールデックス用ビジネスカードのデザインと歴史的価値についてである。コメントでは、カードのロゴや色使い、シンプルさが現代の「ぼんやり」あるいは過剰なグラフィックよりも印象的だと称賛される一方、ロールデックスに挟むと電話番号や住所が切れてしまう可能性があり、上部に配置すれば実用性が向上すると指摘される意見も見られた。また、カードに記載されている名前がフィクションの「フォールアウト」のように聞こえるという懐疑的声と、実際に知人がその会社で働いていたという個人的エピソードが添えられ、歴史と現実の狭間での興味が示された。賛否は主にデザインの美観 versus 実用性の観点で分かれ、一方で史料としての希少性やコレクション価値についてはほぼ全員が肯定的だった。注目すべきコメントとして、「ブラックホール」というサルベージ会社の背景や、名前がフォールアウトのように聞こえるが実際に知人が関わっていたというエピソードが、単なるデザイン論を超えて個人的・文化的なつながりを感じさせた点が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: Los Alamos Rolodex の名刺セレクションは、核開発時代の科学者ネットワークを可視化した貴重な資料だ。日本の研究機関も、過去の学術交流の形態を振り返り、現代の国際共同研究における人的ネットワーク構築の参考にしている。

comments.author: CommenterPerson
comments.text: Here are some things I try: Turn off Notifications. Turn off location services except when navigating or calling the taxi. Uninstall as many apps as possible, use browser. Use adblocking anti tracking browser (I use Duck, alt suggestions welcome). Report unknown / unwanted senders as spam. That said, I am a NEWS ADDICT. There are four world leaders whose downfall I eagerly await, and frequently check the news for this ;-) .. you might be able to guess three but not the fourth.

comments.author: academic_84572
comments.text: For me, adaptive friction has been very helpful - allow access to distracting apps/sites, but make them progressively harder to use. For phones, ScreenZen is great at this. Makes you pause before visiting an app or site, and you can configure the pause to grow each time you use it. You can also set a timeout on the app. Very flexible settings. For desktop, I recently built a free browser extension called MooBlock - it's similar to ScreenZen in that it adds a forced pause before you reach a distracting site. But once you reach the site, a herd of cows start walking all over your screen to make the website less appealing. It's available in both the Chrome and Firefox extension stores. Hoping to make an Android version later this year too. Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/mooblock/eanbagjehd... Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/mooblock/?utm...

comments.author: rglover
comments.text: Putting in blockers and the like helps, but what I've found worked best was to consider this quote by Anthony DeMello: "When you fight something, you're tied to it forever. As long as you're fighting it, you’re giving it power." When I learned to stop feeling bad/guilty/thinking this was a problem to solve and just let my mind drift, I found that my mind naturally learned when it was disciplined work time vs. browse the internet time. Personally, I noticed that when I didn't have any artificial restriction, I was less inclined to waste time on those things. In practice: "oh, my mind doesn't want to do that other thing right now but it does want to go look at this thing; let it." The more I've loosened my grip, the less distractions have affected my productivity.

stories.summary_ja: コメントでは、インターネットを「つまらない」ものにするための具体的な対策が多数提案された。主に議論されたのは、通知や位置情報をオフにし、アプリを削除してブラウザだけに絞る方法、広告・トラッキングブロッカーの利用、そしてScreenZenやMooBlockのように利用前に強制的な待ち時間を設けたり、サイトに牛を歩ませるなどの「適応的摩擦」を導入する手法だ。これに対し、単なるブロックでは根本解決にならず、気分の変化や「闘わない」姿勢が重要だと指摘する意見もあり、Anthony DeMelloの言葉を引用して罪悪感を手放すことで自然にメリハリが生まれるとする考えが支持された。さらに、YouTubeの視聴履歴をオフにすることでレコメンドを断つ方法や、自分自身にキッズアカウントを作ってアクセスを制御し、必要に応じて他者にスクリーンタイム管理を委ねるという極端な手法も話題になった。注目されたのは、待ち時間が増えていくScreenZenの柔軟性と、MooBlockの画面に牛を歩ませるユーモラスなアプローチで、これらは単なる制限ではなく、利用を躊躇させる心理的ハードルとして評価された。
stories.editor_note: インターネットを退屈にする試みは、情報過多と刺激依存へのアンチテーゼとして注目される。日本のデジタルウェルネス分野では、意識的に低刺激環境を作り出すサービスやアプリが増えており、ユーザーのメンタルヘルス改善に寄与すると期待されている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、生物の進化メカニズムを宇宙や多宇宙に適用できるかという点だ。コメントでは「レプリケータ（複製者）がどこにあるのか」「単なる無作為な変化ではなく、選択的に残る違いが必要」といった疑問が提起され、進化のアナロジーを宇宙構造形成に当てはめる妥当性が論じられた。賛同する側は、進化こそ普遍的原理であり、現実だけでなくすべての現実を支配し、進化そのものも進化すると主張し、『The Case Against Reality』やサーガンの『Pale Blue Dot』（惑星の円軌道は早期宇宙での衝突による自然選択の結果）を参照して支持した。逆に懐疑的側は、無限の多宇宙において観測される知性を持つ宇宙が選ばれるという観測者偏滥だけでは説明が不十分で、具体的なレプリケータや遺伝様の機構が示されていないと指摘した。注目されたコメントとして、サーガンの記憶を引き合いに出した惑星軌道の自然選択説と、今回の宇宙選択理論が以前の「Blowtorch Theory」より保守的であるという指摘が挙げられた。これらの議論から、進化のアナロジーは興味深いが、メカニズムの明確化が課題であるというコンセンサスが見られた。
stories.editor_note: 地球の生物は進化によって発達してきた。宇宙も同様に進化したらどうなるか？という思考実験は、宇宙論と複雑系科学の境界を探るものだ。日本の宇宙機関や理論物理学コミュニティは、こうしたシナリオをシミュレーションモデルで検証し、新たな観測戦略のヒントを得ようとしている。

stories.title_en: Product Backlog Problems: Why Your Hierarchy Is Broken
stories.title_ja: プロダクト バックログの問題：なぜあなたの階層が壊れているのか

comments.author: bluGill
comments.text: I'm making a point to be careful what I allow into my backlog. If realistically we're not going to do it, it doesn't belong in the backlog. There are a lot of things I want to do that are not in the backlog because I know realistically they're just not worth it. Even with AI where you are not using your monthly token allowance, there are still a lot of things not worth doing. Just this week I was thinking about an idea that would improve builds, let's do that refactoring. However, as I started looking into the amount of work I would require to get it done, I realized that, yes, it would be an improvement to our builds, but the cost of getting the work done is greater than the improvement is worth, and so I'm not going to go forward with it. It's too bad there are a number of annoyances that I'm going to be living with because it's not worth fixing. But that is the reality of life. I need to do things that will ultimately satisfy our customers that keep coming back and paying us more money.

comments.author: alephnerd
comments.text: Submarine article. Also, back when I was still a PM I found most these kinds of tools to be a waste of time. Tools don't solve ownership. I found just talking directly with my sellers and engineers in the same room would solve these backlog issues. Every project, initiative, and task needed to be directly tied to enhancing customer satisfaction or tangibly driving revenue (1-2% of ARR). If Eng could not justify why a refactor could help customer satisfaction or topline P/L, I'd deprioritize it. If sales could not justify why a checkbox feature would satisfy the majority of our customers or help our topline P/L, I'd deprioritize it and re-prioritize the refactor. Just demand fucking ownership from everyone - PM, Sales, and Engineering - and complex projects can be easily executed. Ownership also means trusting the people executing but also validating - I trusted my engineers, salespeople, and stakeholders and vice versa, but I always made sure to do my homework. Backlogs will always expand - that's to be expected - but someone must groom them and own them. That's on the PM. Who cares what tool you use - it could be JIRA or a Excel 95 spreadsheet. Just own shit and fucking execute.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、バックログに入れるべきは「現実的にやる価値がある」仕事だけであり、コストと効果のバランスを取って見極めるべきだという点。具体的には、リファクタリングや小さな改善アイデアでも、実装にかかる工数が得られる利益を上回る場合は見送るべきだと主張している。さらに、バックログの肥大化を防ぐためには、PMが所有権を持ち、エンジニア・セールス・ステークホルダーがそれぞれの仕事が顧客満足度や収益にどう寄与するかを説明し、それに基づいて優先順位をつけることが重要だと指摘している。ツール（JIRAやExcelなど）は本質ではなく、所有者が明確であればどの手段でも構わないという考えも示されている。

賛否両論として、コメント自体は所有権と直接対話の重要性を強調しているが、一方でツールを完全に否定する stance に対して、ツールが可視化や距離があるチームの調整に役立つという反論がコミュニティで見られる可能性がある。また、すべてのアイデアをバックログに残しておくことで将来の機会を逃さないという考え方と、今回の「やらない」決断の間に意見が分かれる点も挙げられる。

注目コメントは、投稿者自身の実体験に基づく具体的な例（ビルド改善のリファクタリングをコストが高いため見送った話）と、「所有者に責任を持たせればツールは何でもよい」という結論であり、バックログ管理における実践的な指針として特に洞察に富んでいると考えられる。
stories.editor_note: プロダクト バックログの問題：なぜあなたの階層が壊れているのか は、アジャイル開発における優先順位付けの崩壊を指摘する。日本のソフトウェア企業でも、スケールアップに伴いバックログの肥大化と可視化の難しさが課題となっており、見直しの必要性が叫ばれている。

comments.author: r3trohack3r
comments.text: Tangentially related, I applied a similar approach to compress the npm registry by over 90% on disk a few years back. Since most versions of a package are similar, you can delta encode them first and then compress them. The deltas are small and compress well as a collection with the original source files. For another use case, prior to compressing, I’ve applied a rolling hash to deterministically split the file. Then compressed the chunks and stored them in a CID filesystem. The result is that files that are largely similar share compressed chunks. There are a lot of things we can do to be substantially more efficient with the computers we have, but engineers often cost more than hardware. With recent supply chain constraints that calculus is changing!

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Zstandard と Pingora を用いてキャッシュを圧縮し、ストレージや帯域幅を削減できるかという点だ。コメントでは、パッケージレジストリ（npm、PyPI など）でほぼ同じバージョンが多いため、デルタエンコードやローリングハッシュでチャンクに分割し、共通部分を圧縮して再利用すれば90％以上のディスク削減が可能だと指摘されている。一方で、圧縮したデータをそのまま配信するか、クライアントが対応していればオン・ザ・フライでトランスコードするか、あるいは人気コンテンツだけに限定すべきかという意見が分かれた。特にレンジリクエストへの影響については、圧縮前ならキャッシュから一部を直接読めるが、圧縮後はどう扱うのかという疑問が注目され、「range requests remain unchanged」という主張に対する説明不足が指摘された。さらに、エンジニアのコストがハードウェアより高いという従来の考え方がサプライチェーン制約で変わりつつあるという観察も挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: Zstandard と Pingora を使えばキャッシュ ストレージをペタバイト単位で節約できる という主張は、圧縮効率とプロキシ性能の組み合わせによるインフラ最適化を示す。日本の大規模ウェブサービスやクラウドプロバイダーは、TCO 削減のため同様の技術スタックの導入を検討しており、今後の採用動向が注目される。
